chief_complaint: sudden severe throat swelling, wheezing, diffuse hives, and cardiovascular collapse within 10 minutes of multiple bee stings
hpi_details: 28M presenting in acute Type I IgE-mediated anaphylactic shock with angioedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension requiring immediate intramuscular Epinephrine (0.3-0.5 mg of 1:1000 into anterolateral thigh), IV fluid bolus, and adjunctive antihistamines/corticosteroids.
ideas: He thinks the swarm injected too much venom into his body all at once and it is poisoning his system.
concerns: He is terrified that his throat will close up completely before he can take another breath.
expectations: He hopes to get an immediate injection to bring down the swelling so his airway opens up.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Anaphylactic Shock (bee sting) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Anaphylactic Shock (bee sting) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate intramuscular epinephrine as first-line therapy, with airway support, IV fluid resuscitation, and adjunctive antihistamines/corticosteroids, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden severe throat swelling, wheezing, diffuse hives, and cardiovascular collapse within 10 minutes of multiple bee stings

Key HPI features: 28M presenting in acute Type I IgE-mediated anaphylactic shock with angioedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension requiring immediate intramuscular Epinephrine (0.3-0.5 mg of 1:1000 into anterolateral thigh), IV fluid bolus, and adjunctive antihistamines/corticosteroids.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 132 (tachycardia), BP 78/45 (hypotension/distributive shock), RR 28, SpO2 90% on room air. Diffuse urticarial rash across trunk and extremities with angioedema of the lips and tongue. Audible inspiratory stridor and bilateral expiratory wheeze on auscultation. Skin cool and mottled with delayed capillary refill. Multiple visible sting sites on the forearm.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Anaphylactic Shock (bee sting).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vasovagal reaction to the sting without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Throat swelling or wheezing — treat as anaphylaxis, give epinephrine now.
management_principles: Immediate first-line therapy: intramuscular Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed; position patient supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress dictates otherwise) and give high-flow supplemental oxygen

Establish IV access and give rapid crystalloid fluid bolus for hypotension; administer adjunctive IV H1 blocker (diphenhydramine) and H2 blocker (famotidine), IV corticosteroids (methylprednisolone), and nebulized bronchodilators for persistent bronchospasm
Observe for a minimum of 4-6 hours to monitor for biphasic reaction; discharge with a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, written action plan, and allergy/immunology follow-up
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 28M presenting with sudden severe throat swelling, wheezing, diffuse hives, and cardiovascular collapse within 10 minutes of multiple bee stings, classic for anaphylactic shock (Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction).

reference_soap.assessment: Anaphylactic Shock secondary to multiple bee stings, with angioedema, bronchospasm, and distributive hypotension.
reference_soap.plan: STAT emergency anaphylaxis protocol: 1. Immediate first-line therapy: intramuscular Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed; position patient supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress dictates otherwise) and give high-flow supplemental oxygen. 2. Establish IV access and give rapid crystalloid fluid bolus for hypotension; administer adjunctive IV H1 blocker (diphenhydramine) and H2 blocker (famotidine), IV corticosteroids (methylprednisolone), and nebulized bronchodilators for persistent bronchospasm. 3. Observe for a minimum of 4-6 hours to monitor for biphasic reaction; discharge with a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, written action plan, and allergy/immunology follow-up.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical criteria for anaphylaxis (acute onset of skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise or hypotension after a likely allergen exposure) and distinguish it from a large local sting reaction or vasovagal response
Understand that intramuscular epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh is the immediate, first-line, life-saving treatment and must never be delayed for antihistamines or corticosteroids alone
Execute supportive resuscitation for anaphylactic shock, including positioning, high-flow oxygen, IV crystalloid resuscitation for hypotension, and adjunctive H1/H2 blockers and corticosteroids
Counsel patients on biphasic reaction risk, post-event observation, and discharge with a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector and allergist referral

teaching.one_liner: A systemic IgE-mediated reaction to insect venom causing throat swelling, wheezing, hives, and cardiovascular collapse within minutes — treated immediately with intramuscular epinephrine, the only drug that reverses it.
red_flags: Throat swelling or wheezing — treat as anaphylaxis, give epinephrine now

must_ask.say: How many times were you stung, and how soon after did symptoms start?
Does your throat feel tight, or is it hard to breathe?
Do you have hives all over your body?
Have you ever reacted this way to a sting before?
Do you carry an epinephrine auto-injector, and has it been used?

history.answer: I was stung by several bees about fifteen minutes ago, and now my throat is swelling shut and I can barely breathe.
It started very suddenly, about five to ten minutes after I got stung, and it has been getting worse by the minute.
It is extremely severe. I am gasping for air even while sitting completely still.
The throat tightness and breathing trouble have been nonstop and rapidly getting worse. I have never experienced anything like this before.
I feel like I'm suffocating if I try to lie flat, so I have to sit upright. I did not wake up choking from sleep.
I was stung while trimming hedges in my garden. Cold air, exercise, dust, or animals have never triggered breathing trouble for me.
Yes, I can hear a high-pitched whistling sound when I breathe out and a loud choking noise in my throat when I try to inhale.
I have a dry choking cough because my throat feels closed, but no phlegm and no fever or chills.
My chest feels tight and constricted like a heavy band is wrapped around it, but there is no sharp or stabbing pain.
My heart is pounding and racing very fast. I feel extremely dizzy and faint, like I am about to pass out.
No, I haven't coughed up any blood.
No, my legs and feet are not swollen, and my weight has not changed.
Neither of my legs is swollen or painful. I haven't been on any long flights, haven't been immobilized, and haven't had any surgery.
I haven't felt unusually tired lately, and I haven't noticed any bleeding, bruising, or dark black stools.
My hands feel slightly numb and tingly, and I feel terrified because I can't get enough air, but this definitely didn't start from panic or hyperventilation.
I do not have asthma, COPD, heart failure, or any history of heart attacks. I have never been prescribed an inhaler.
I work an office job in software, so I have no exposure to industrial dust, asbestos, birds, or mold.
I take medication for high blood pressure, but I do not take beta-blockers, aspirin, ibuprofen, or any other pain relievers.
I accidentally hit a bee nest while gardening about fifteen minutes ago and was stung three or four times on my right forearm.
My lips and tongue feel swollen and thick, and my throat feels like it is completely closing off when I try to swallow.
Yes, intensely itchy raised red hives broke out across my chest, stomach, and arms right after the stings.
I was stung once as a young child and only had a small red bump that itched for a couple of days. I never had a widespread reaction like this.
No, I have never had an EpiPen prescribed, so I haven't received or injected any epinephrine.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, but no other chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once daily for my blood pressure. I don't take any supplements or over-the-counter drugs.
I have no known drug allergies and no food allergies. It looks like I am severely allergic to bees now.
I am a lifelong non-smoker and have never used tobacco or electronic cigarettes.
I drink socially, maybe one or two beers on weekends, and I haven't had any alcohol today.
I work as a software engineer and live in an apartment with my wife.
My father has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of severe allergies, asthma, or early heart disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 78/45 mmHg, heart rate 132 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C.
Patient is in acute respiratory distress, visibly gasping, diaphoretic, using accessory neck muscles, and demonstrating audible stridor; skin appears cool and mottled.
Marked angioedema with prominent swelling of the lips and tongue, and significant edema of the uvula and posterior oropharynx.
Internal jugular veins are flat with no jugular venous distention.
Tachypneic chest expansion with prominent intercostal retractions and suprasternal notching; no chest wall tenderness or crepitus.
Resonant percussion notes symmetrically throughout both hemithoraces.
Audible inspiratory stridor loudest over the anterior neck, with widespread diffuse expiratory wheezes across all lung zones bilaterally.
Marked tachycardia with regular rhythm; normal heart sounds with no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are weak and thready bilaterally, with delayed capillary refill time of four seconds.
Diffuse erythematous urticarial plaques across trunk and extremities, with multiple distinct puncture marks and localized erythematous swelling on the right forearm.
No pretibial or ankle pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Both calves are symmetric, soft, and non-tender without swelling, erythema, or palpable cords.
